learn.title: Floating Solar Farms: Power on Water
learn.intro: Floating photovoltaic (FPV) systems sit on reservoirs, lakes, and oceans, generating clean electricity while saving precious water. As land becomes scarce, this dual-use approach offers a powerful path for countries like India, where water and energy security are tightly linked.
learn.c1_text: Floating solar panels are mounted on buoyant structures anchored to the waterbed. Like lily pads on a pond, they convert sunlight into electricity while floating. A typical 100 MW floating plant can occupy roughly 200 acres of water surface, much less land than ground-mounted equivalents of the same capacity.
learn.c2_text: Water beneath the panels keeps them 3–5°C cooler than rooftop systems, boosting efficiency by roughly 5–12%. Think of it like a car engine running cooler performs better. The modules also reduce water evaporation by up to 70%, a critical advantage for drought-prone reservoirs used for drinking water supply.
learn.c3_text: India's Omkareshwar Dam in Madhya Pradesh hosts one of the world's largest floating solar plants at 600 MW capacity, commissioned under NTPC's renewable expansion. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has set a target of 10 GW of floating solar, recognizing water-energy co-benefits in Indian hydropower reservoirs.

learn.stat2: Floating solar cuts water evaporation by up to 70%
learn.stat3: FPV systems gain 5–12% efficiency from water cooling

learn.title: The Duck Curve: Solar's Sunset Challenge
learn.intro: As solar energy floods the grid at midday, conventional power plants must ramp down, then suddenly ramp back up when the sun sets. This creates a net-load curve shaped like a duck, posing one of the most complex operational puzzles for the modern electricity grid worldwide.
learn.c1_title: Why the Curve Looks Like a Duck 🦆
learn.c1_text: Imagine a busy restaurant: lunch crowd needs food at noon, then suddenly everyone orders dinner at 6 PM. Solar serves lunch generously but leaves before dinner. The gap between solar generation and evening demand forces utilities to fire up fast-ramping gas plants just when renewables disappear.
learn.c2_text: In California, net demand can ramp up by roughly 13 GW in just three hours around sunset. Traditional coal and nuclear plants cannot respond this fast. Utilities increasingly rely on battery storage, demand response, and flexible gas turbines to keep lights on during the steep evening climb of the duck's neck.
learn.c3_text: India's duck curve is sharpening in states like Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, where solar penetration exceeds 15% of daily demand. The Central Electricity Authority recommends battery energy storage systems of 42 GWh by 2030, alongside forecasting tools, to manage evening ramps when 70+ GW of solar drops off simultaneously.
learn.stat1: California duck ramp: ~13 GW in 3 hours at sunset
learn.stat2: California solar met ~20% of annual demand in 2023
learn.stat3: India targets 42 GWh of battery storage by 2030
learn.stat4: Net-load peak shifted from late afternoon to evening hours

learn.title: Demand Response: Smart Load Balancing
learn.intro: Demand response programs pay large electricity users to reduce or shift consumption during peak hours. Instead of building new power plants, we use existing electricity more wisely, turning factories, ACs, and even EV chargers into flexible grid resources that stabilize renewable-heavy systems.
learn.c1_text: Instead of lighting a new coal plant for one hot evening, demand response asks aluminium smelters to pause production and offices to pre-cool buildings. Like dimming household bulbs during a dinner party, it spreads electricity use so the grid never gets overwhelmed, saving money and emissions.
learn.c2_text: Modern demand response uses smart meters, IoT thermostats, and automated signals sent seconds before grid stress. Industrial facilities can shed 1–10 MW within minutes, earning payments of $100–$500 per MW-hour reduced. Aggregators bundle thousands of small users, replicating a virtual power plant from rooftops and basements.
learn.c3_text: India's peak electricity demand crossed 240 GW in summer 2024, with shortages of 4–6 GW common during evenings. The Ministry of Power launched the 'Peak Demand Management' program, encouraging industrial consumers, data centres, and even agricultural pumps to participate in time-of-day pricing, reducing costly peaker plant reliance.

learn.title: Second Life EV Batteries: Grid Storage Gold
learn.intro: Electric vehicle batteries retire when capacity drops to 70–80%, but they still hold 15+ kWh of useful energy. Repurposing them for grid storage creates affordable, sustainable batteries that extend a pack's life by another decade, turning automotive waste into renewable energy infrastructure.
learn.c1_text: Think of an EV battery like a smartphone: after two years it struggles to last a day, but still works fine as a bedside clock. Similarly, a 60 kWh Nissan Leaf pack losing driving range still stores 45 kWh, enough to power a small home for three days or stabilize a neighbourhood microgrid reliably.
learn.c2_text: Engineers test each module for internal resistance, capacity, and self-discharge. Healthy cells are regrouped into stationary packs, while degraded cells are recycled. Second-life systems cost roughly 30–50% less than new lithium-ion storage, though they offer shorter cycle life of 1,000–2,000 cycles compared to 4,000+ for new packs.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 30% EV penetration by 2030, creating millions of retiring batteries. IIT Madras researchers are piloting second-life packs for solar irrigation pumps in Tamil Nadu. Companies like Lohum Cleantech and Tata Chemicals are building reverse-logistics networks to repurpose batteries for rural microgrids and telecom towers across India.
learn.stat2: Second-life storage costs 30–50% less than new packs

learn.title: Small Wind Turbines for Homes and Communities
learn.intro: Small wind turbines, typically 1–100 kW, bring wind power to farms, schools, and remote communities. Unlike industrial wind farms, they operate close to where electricity is used, offering energy independence for rural India, off-grid homes, and small businesses seeking clean, reliable power.
learn.c1_text: Small wind turbines use lift, the same force that makes airplane wings fly. Wind passing over angled blades creates a pressure difference, spinning the rotor. A typical 10 kW residential turbine standing 18 metres tall can generate 10,000–25,000 kWh annually, enough to power 2–4 Indian homes each year.
learn.c2_text: Small wind needs average wind speeds above 4–5 m/s. Like sailing, the smoother the wind, the more energy captured. Open hills, coastlines, and ridge tops perform best. Urban sites suffer from turbulent buildings reducing output by 20–40%, making careful siting more important than turbine quality alone.
learn.c3_text: India installed over 4,000 small wind turbines in states like Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and Maharashtra, primarily for agricultural pumps and remote telecom towers. The MNRE's small wind program subsidizes 50% of capital costs in special-category states, helping remote Himalayan villages and Lakshadweep islands achieve energy self-sufficiency.
learn.stat3: Minimum wind speed: 4–5 m/s for viability
learn.readLabel: Explore at US Dept of Energy

learn.title: HVDC Transmission: Power Across Continents
learn.intro: High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) lines transport electricity across thousands of kilometres with only 3% loss per 1,000 km, half the losses of AC lines. They link distant solar parks in Rajasthan, offshore wind in Gujarat, and hydropower in Bhutan into one national supergrid.
learn.c1_title: Why DC Beats AC for Distance ⚡
learn.c1_text: Alternating current loses energy to skin effect and reactive power over long cables, like a long garden hose losing water pressure. DC current flows smoothly with no waste heat from oscillations. A 2,000 km HVDC line loses only 6% of energy, while AC loses 15–20%, making DC the obvious choice for cross-country links.
learn.c2_text: HVDC needs expensive converter stations using thyristors or IGBTs to switch between AC and DC, costing $100–300 million each. But the savings on long cables justify the investment. The 720 km North Sea Link, a 1,400 MW cable between Norway and the UK, powers 1.4 million UK homes with Norwegian hydropower.
learn.c3_text: India operates over 20,000 circuit km of HVDC lines, including the 2,500 km ±800 kV Raigarh–Pugalur link transmitting 6,000 MW from Chhattisgarh to Tamil Nadu. PowerGrid is planning new HVDC corridors to evacuate 175 GW of renewable energy by 2030 from remote deserts and Himalayan hydro plants to load centres.
learn.stat1: HVDC loss: ~3% per 1,000 km versus 7–10% for AC
learn.stat3: North Sea Link: 1,400 MW subsea cable to UK
